title: India's Factories Are Cooling Off. The Warning Signs Are Hard to Ignore.
excerpt: Manufacturing growth slipped to its second-weakest pace in four years in June, with export orders at a 39-month low and hiring at its softest this year — even as KPIT Technologies crashed 17% on a European demand shock.
body:
India's manufacturing engine, long celebrated as the brightest spot in Asia's growth story, is showing signs of strain that investors and policymakers can no longer wave away.

The HSBC India Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index fell to 54.2 in June from 55.0 in May, coming in below the preliminary estimate of 54.5. It was the second-weakest reading since mid-2022, with only March's figure worse in the past four years. The index still signals expansion — anything above 50 does — but the direction of travel is unmistakable.

"The moderation suggests demand has cooled slightly after the earlier surge linked to the Middle East conflict," said Pranjul Bhandari, Chief India Economist at HSBC. "Growth slowed across output, new orders, export orders and employment, with international sales recording their weakest increase since March 2023."

## Export Orders: The European Problem

The most concerning signal in the June data was export orders, which grew at their weakest pace in 39 months. Firms repeatedly pointed to subdued demand from European clients — a complaint that has been building for quarters but is now showing up forcefully in the numbers.

Europe's manufacturing sector remains mired in its own difficulties. The war-driven energy shock, weak consumer demand, and a painful EV transition have squeezed margins for automakers and industrial firms across the continent. Those pressures are now cascading into India's supply chains.

Nowhere was this more visible than in the 17% crash of KPIT Technologies on Wednesday, which wiped the Pune-based automotive software company's stock to a near four-year low. KPIT warned that its first-quarter dollar revenue would decline approximately 1% year-on-year, blaming "abrupt spending cuts by several European automotive OEMs." The company said the impact was not anticipated and came to light only in recent weeks.

JPMorgan cut KPIT's earnings estimates by 9–22% and warned that the first half of fiscal 2027 is likely to remain weak, with sequential revenue growth expected only by the fourth quarter. The selloff dragged peers like Tata Elxsi along with it, rattling the broader automotive engineering sector.

## Hiring Hits a Wall

The PMI data also flagged a worrying slowdown in job creation. Employment expanded at its weakest pace this year, with 97% of surveyed firms keeping headcount unchanged. Companies cited adequate capacity and a general absence of pressure to add workers — not exactly the language of a booming industrial base.

Business confidence fell to a five-month low, with firms expressing concern over demand conditions and market competition.

## The Silver Lining: Inflation Pressure Is Easing

Not everything in the PMI was bleak. Input cost inflation eased to a four-month low, and output charges rose at their slowest rate in three months, with 93% of companies holding prices flat from May. The easing is partly a function of falling oil prices — Brent crude has crashed 43% from its Iran-war peak of $126 per barrel in April to around $72 — which is a direct tailwind for India's cost structure.

For consumers, the easing price environment may eventually translate into softer inflation and more room for the Reserve Bank of India to support growth.

## Context: Still Expanding, Still Vulnerable

It is worth noting that India's manufacturing sector is still growing. A PMI of 54.2 is in line with the long-run series average and comfortably in expansion territory. Compared to Europe, where several economies are flirting with contraction, India's industrial base remains resilient.

But the trajectory matters. New orders rose at their second-weakest rate since June 2022. Capital goods output — a proxy for corporate investment intentions — was particularly soft. And the European demand weakness is not cyclical noise; it reflects structural pressures in India's largest developed-market export destination.

India has built its manufacturing ambitions on becoming a global supply chain alternative to China. That strategy requires healthy demand from the very markets now pulling back. If European automakers and industrial firms continue to retrench, the downstream impact on India's IT services, engineering outsourcing, and parts manufacturing sectors will deepen.

## What NRIs Should Watch

For diaspora investors who have piled into India's equity rally — the market just reclaimed $5 trillion in capitalisation — the PMI data is a reminder that the macro picture is mixed. The oil crash and falling bond yields are genuine positives. But manufacturing momentum is fading at precisely the moment when corporate earnings need to justify elevated valuations.

The next data point to watch is July's PMI, due in early August. If the monsoon disappoints further — June was the fifth-driest since 1901 — rural demand could weaken, adding another headwind. For now, India's factory floor is still humming. But the hum is getting quieter.
